title: Light & the Spectrum
intro: Light is energy carried by electric and magnetic waves, and also by tiny particles called photons. Learn how light meets matter, how wavelength and frequency are linked by c = λf, how photon energy depends on frequency, and how the electromagnetic spectrum runs from gamma rays to radio waves.

sections.title: Light carries energy

img.alt: The Sun shining brightly in a blue sky with clouds and trees around it.

steps.title: Sunlight is energy on the move
bullets: Light has energy, called **radiative energy**. You feel it when sunlight warms your skin: the skin absorbs the light and its molecules move faster.
We care about how fast light delivers energy. That rate is **power**, measured in **watts** (W), and 1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s).
The Sun's power output is **3.8 x 10^26 W**. A 100 W light bulb uses 100 joules of energy every second it is on.

steps.title: Light thins out with distance
bullets: Light from a source spreads out in every direction, so the farther you are, the thinner the light is spread.
The energy arriving on each square metre falls with the **square of the distance**: twice as far gives 1/4 as much, three times as far gives 1/9 as much.
Example: Mercury is 0.387 times as far from the Sun as Earth. It gets 1 / 0.387^2 = about 6.7 times more sunlight on each square metre than Earth does.

boxes.text: Why use watts instead of joules? A joule is an amount of energy, like a bucket of water. A watt is how fast the bucket is being poured. We cannot hold light in our hands, so the flow rate is the useful number.
Watt = Joule per second. A 100 W bulb eats 100 J every second, so after 10 seconds it has used 1,000 J.

Power is a rate, not a total. '3.8 x 10^26 W' means 3.8 x 10^26 joules EVERY SECOND, not a total amount of energy. Textbook 5.1 gives the 100 W bulb example; the 3.8 x 10^26 W value is from slide 2. The inverse-square law for light is not on the slide; it comes from the textbook (Math Insight 10.1, Mercury 0.387 AU).

Why does light fall off as 1/d^2? A source sends out its power in all directions. At twice the distance that same power covers a sphere with 4 times the area, so each square metre gets only 1/4 of the energy.

sourceNotes: Ch5.1 slide 2

sections.title: White light is a mix of colours

img.alt: A beam of white light passing through a glass prism and fanning out into a rainbow.

steps.title: A prism splits white light
bullets: Sunlight (white light) is a mix of many colours, which means many different wavelengths.
A glass prism uses **refraction** (bending of light) to spread the colours apart into a rainbow called a **spectrum**.
Newton proved the colours come from the light, not the prism: when only red light goes into a second prism, only red light comes out.

boxes.text: Why does a prism make a rainbow? The colours in white light travel together, but each colour is bent by a slightly different amount when it goes through glass. That sends each colour in its own direction, so they fan out.
A prism is a colour sorter: it does not make colours, it only separates the ones already hiding in white light.

A prism does not add colour. A second prism on one colour gives the same colour back (Newton, textbook 5.2). Any white light (a bulb as well as the Sun) gives a rainbow through a prism. Practice test 2 Q22 (bulb through a prism) has the explained answer 'rainbow with more red than the Sun's', which needs Wien's law (a later topic); the part that belongs here is: it is still a continuous rainbow, not lines and not one colour.

sections.title: Light and matter: seven interactions

img.alt: A grid of six small diagrams showing light being transmitted, reflected, refracted, diffracted, absorbed and scattered.

steps.title: Six pictures of what matter does to light
bullets: Matter can emit, transmit, reflect, refract, absorb, scatter or diffract light. The grid draws six of these; emission is simply an object giving off light, such as a bulb or the Sun.
**Transmission**: light passes straight through (glass, air). **Absorption**: the light's energy is taken in, often as heat (your hand near a bulb).
**Refraction**: light bends as it enters a new material. **Diffraction**: light spreads out after a narrow gap.

img.alt: On the left a mirror sends a ray off at the same angle it arrived; on the right a movie screen sends light from the projector to every seat in the theatre.

steps.title: Mirror versus movie screen
bullets: **Reflection**: light bounces off in one general direction. A mirror sends a ray off at the same angle it came in (50 degrees in, 50 degrees out in the picture).
**Scattering**: light bounces off in many directions. A movie screen scatters the projector's light so every person in the room sees the whole picture.
Printed pages scatter light too, which is why you can read them from different angles and distances.

img.alt: A room with a lamp, a red chair, a mirror and a window, and snow and a tree outside, with labels showing where light is emitted, reflected, scattered, absorbed and transmitted.

steps.title: Why objects have colours
bullets: A red chair looks red because it scatters red light and absorbs all the other colours. A green lawn scatters green and absorbs the rest.
Under red light only, a green object absorbs the red and sends nothing back, so it looks black.
**Transparent** materials transmit light and **opaque** materials absorb it. Many things are partly both, like dark sunglasses (they absorb more and transmit less than clear glasses).

boxes.text: Why is the daytime sky bright and why are shadows not pitch black? Air molecules scatter sunlight in every direction, bouncing some into the shade. In space there is no air to scatter light, so shadows and the sky are pitch black.
A mirror gives one neat bounce (reflection). A movie screen sprays light everywhere (scattering), which is why everyone in the room sees the picture.

Slide 4 lists SEVEN interactions, but the textbook (5.1) describes four basic ones: emission, absorption, transmission and reflection/scattering. Refraction and diffraction are only drawn on the slide, not defined in the textbook. Practice test 2 Q17: a green object looks black under red light because it ABSORBS the red (answer b), not because it reflects red or absorbs green.

sections.title: Light is an electromagnetic wave

img.alt: A light wave drawn in three dimensions, with a red electric field and a blue magnetic field wiggling at right angles to each other and to the direction the wave moves.

steps.title: Electric and magnetic fields wave together
bullets: Light is a wave made of an **electric field** and a **magnetic field** that wiggle at right angles to each other and to the direction the light travels.
A field tells you how strong a push a charged particle would feel at each spot. Light pushes on charged particles through these fields.
Unlike pond or sound waves, light does not need any material to travel through. Nothing moves up and down in space; the fields vibrate.

img.alt: A wave drawn along an arrow, with labels for the wavelength between two peaks, the frequency at one point, and the speed of light.

steps.title: Wavelength, frequency and speed in light
bullets: The wavelength of light is the distance between adjacent peaks of the electric field (and the magnetic field).
The frequency is the number of times each second that the field vibrates up and down at any one point.
All light travels through empty space at the same speed, **c = 300,000 km/s**.

boxes.text: Why can light cross empty space? Pond waves need water and sound needs air, because they are the vibrations of matter. Light is the vibration of electric and magnetic fields, which exist even where there is no matter. Waves carry energy, not matter: a leaf on a pond only bobs up and down as waves pass.
Electro + magnetic = electromagnetic: two partners that always wiggle together at 90 degrees.
Do not say light needs air or any medium, and do not say light carries matter along with it. Slide 2: 'perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields'.

sourceNotes: Ch5.2 slide 2
Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (pp. 140-141, Figure 5.4 pond waves, Figure 5.5, 'Light as an Electromagnetic Wave')

sections.title: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency, speed

img.alt: Two waves with the same height: a blue one with a longer wavelength and lower frequency and a green one with a shorter wavelength and higher frequency, both moving at the same speed.

steps.title: Reading a wave diagram
bullets: **Amplitude** is the maximum height of a wave peak (it is related to brightness). **Wavelength** is the distance between two peaks.
**Frequency** is the number of peaks that pass a spot each second. It is measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz = 1 peak per second.
Wave speed = wavelength x frequency (v = λ x f). In the picture wave A has the longer wavelength and so the smaller frequency, while both have the same amplitude and speed.

img.alt: A person throwing a pebble into a pond, with ripples spreading outward, labels for peak, trough and wavelength, and a leaf bobbing up and down.

steps.title: A pond example with numbers
bullets: If a leaf bobs up and down 3 times each second, the frequency is 3 Hz, because 3 peaks pass every second.
If each wavelength is 1 cm, each peak moves 1 cm, and 3 peaks pass per second, so the speed is 1 cm x 3 per second = 3 cm/s.
The rule v = λ x f works for any wave: sound, water and light.

boxes.text: Why does speed = wavelength x frequency? In one second, f peaks go past. Each peak has travelled one wavelength to get there, so the wave has moved f x λ in one second. That distance per second is the speed.
Wavelength = the Width of one wave. Frequency = how Frequently peaks arrive.

Frequency is peaks per second, not the distance between peaks (that is wavelength) and not the height (amplitude). Practice test 2 Q20 asks which property counts peaks per second: frequency. Waves with different frequencies can still have the same speed (slide 3 picture).

sourceNotes: Ch5.2 slide 3

sections.title: The light relation c = λf

img.alt: Three waves drawn one above the other: 1 cm wavelength at 30 GHz, half a centimetre at 60 GHz and a quarter of a centimetre at 120 GHz.

steps.title: Longer wave, lower frequency
bullets: For all light, **c = λf**: the speed of light equals wavelength times frequency. In empty space c is about 300,000 km/s (3 x 10^8 m/s).
Because c never changes, a longer wavelength must mean a lower frequency, and a shorter wavelength a higher frequency.
In the picture, 1 cm gives 30 GHz. Half the wavelength (0.5 cm) gives double the frequency (60 GHz). A quarter of the wavelength (0.25 cm) gives four times the frequency (120 GHz). 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.

steps.title: Solving for frequency or wavelength
bullets: Rearrange: f = c / λ and λ = c / f. First change units to metres and hertz: 1 nm = 10^-9 m, 1 MHz = 10^6 Hz, 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.
A radio station at 93.3 MHz = 93.3 x 10^6 Hz: λ = (3 x 10^8 m/s) / (93.3 x 10^6 Hz) = 3.2 m. That is why radio antennas must be fairly long.

boxes.text: Why can't wavelength and frequency both go up? Their product must always equal c. If wavelength doubles, frequency must halve to keep the product the same. It is like walking at a fixed speed: longer steps means fewer steps per second.
Seesaw: wavelength goes up, frequency goes down. Their product c stays put in the middle.

Slide 4 gives the formula c = λf but no number for c. The textbook gives c = 3 x 10^8 m/s (300,000 km/s); use it. The most common mistake is the power of 10: convert nm, MHz and GHz first. Slide 3 uses v = λf for any wave; for light v is c.

sourceNotes: Ch5.2 slide 4

sections.title: Wavelength sets the colour

img.alt: A column of colours from violet to dark red, each with a drawn wave and its wavelength in nanometres, getting longer toward red.

steps.title: Colours and their wavelengths
bullets: Our eyes see wavelengths from about **400 nm** (violet) to about **700 nm** (dark red). 1 nm = one billionth of a metre.
The picture labels: violet 400, indigo 425, blue 470, aqua 490, green 550, yellow 600, orange 630, red 665, dark red 700 nm. The picture also shows angstroms: 10 Å = 1 nm.
Longer wavelength (lower frequency) means redder light. Shorter wavelength (higher frequency) means bluer light.

boxes.text: Why is red 'low frequency'? By c = λf, the colour with the longest visible wavelength has the smallest frequency. Red has the longest visible wavelength, so it has the lowest frequency of the visible colours.
Red is Relaxed (long, lazy waves, low energy). Violet is Vigorous (short, fast waves, high energy).

Slide 5 shows nine colour labels (with indigo and aqua). The textbook names the basic colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, and puts 400 nm at the blue/violet end and 700 nm at the red end. Use the slide's numbers. The RED end has the LONGER wavelength; many students flip this.

sourceNotes: Ch5.2 slide 5
Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 142, 'The light that our eyes can see...', 400 to 700 nm) and 5.1 (p. 138, basic colours)

images.alt: A column of colours from violet to dark red, each with a drawn wave and its wavelength in nanometres, getting longer toward red.

sections.title: Light is also a particle: photons

steps.title: Photon energy formulas
bullets: Experiments in the early 1900s showed that light also behaves like a particle. A particle of light is a **photon**, and each photon has a wavelength, a frequency and a speed.
Photon energy: **E = hf** or **E = hc/λ**, where h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s is Planck's constant.
Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energy per photon. Lower frequency (longer wavelength) means less.

steps.title: Photon energy with numbers
bullets: That is tiny: barely a billion-trillionth of the 100 J a 100 W bulb uses each second. A bulb sends out huge numbers of photons.
If the wavelength doubles, f halves and E halves. If the wavelength drops to one-third, f triples and E triples.

boxes.text: Why does a short wavelength mean more energy? E = hf, so energy rises with frequency, and by c = λf a short wavelength means a high frequency. That is why ultraviolet can harm skin cells but radio waves do nothing to the body.
E goes with f (both up together) but against λ (E = hc/λ: big wavelength, small energy). 'Big f, big E; big λ, small E.'

Energy per photon is not the same as brightness or power. All photons travel at the same speed c whatever their energy: radio waves are not slower than X-rays (ASTR207 practice Q22 answer b; Q23: X-rays have the highest photon energy of the list; Q24: wavelength doubles gives frequency halved and energy halved, derived from c = λf and E = hf).

sections.title: How light pushes charges around

img.alt: A row of electrons drawn as dots along a wavy line, bobbing up and down as a light wave passes.

steps.title: Electrons bob as light passes
bullets: Light interacts with charged particles, mostly **electrons**, through its electric and magnetic fields. A passing light wave makes electrons bob up and down.
Often atoms and molecules absorb the light and turn its energy into heat.
Sometimes an atom absorbs a photon and sends it out again in a different direction. Other times the light just changes direction because of the electrons.

boxes.text: Why does sunlight warm your skin? Electrons in your skin soak up the light's energy and pass it on as faster molecular motion, which is heat.
Light is the wave on the pond and electrons are the leaves: they bob as it goes by.
The electrons only bob up and down. They are not carried along with the light; only energy travels. Slide 7's picture is Figure 5.5a of the textbook.

sourceNotes: Ch5.2 slide 7
Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 141, Figure 5.5a)

sections.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
sections.slides: Ch5.2: 8 and 1 (spectrum figure from textbook Figure 5.7)

img.alt: The electromagnetic spectrum drawn as a wave that stretches from gamma rays on the left to radio waves on the right, with scales for wavelength, frequency and energy and everyday objects showing the size of each wavelength.

steps.title: From gamma rays to radio waves
bullets: The **electromagnetic spectrum** is the full range of light, in order: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves.
Going from gamma rays to radio waves, wavelength gets longer while frequency and energy get lower. Gamma rays: shortest, most energy. Radio: longest, least energy.
The size scale in the picture runs from a hydrogen atom (X-rays and gamma rays) up to a football field (radio waves). Visible light sits just below 10^-6 m.

img.alt: An X-ray picture of two hands showing the bones.

steps.title: What different light does
bullets: X-ray photons carry enough energy to pass through skin and muscle, but bones and teeth block them, so X-ray pictures show bones.
Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to damage skin cells (sunburn). Radio photons carry so little energy that they have no effect on the body.
Warm objects give off infrared (so we link infrared with heat). Radio waves make electrons move in an antenna, which is how radio communication works.

img.alt: Rows of pictures showing sources of each kind of light on Earth, such as radioactive elements, X-ray machines, light bulbs, people, radar, microwave ovens and radio transmitters, and in space, such as gamma-ray bursts, the Sun and the cosmic microwave background.

steps.title: Where each kind of light comes from
bullets: Sources on Earth in the picture: radioactive elements, X-ray machines, light bulbs, people, radar, microwave ovens, radio transmitters.
Sources in space: gamma-ray bursts, black hole accretion disks, the Sun, planets and star-forming clouds, the cosmic microwave background, radio galaxies.

steps.title: One family of light
bullets: Every kind of light travels at the speed of light. Only wavelength, frequency and energy per photon differ.
Our eyes see only a tiny slice. The reddest red has only about twice the wavelength of the bluest blue (700 nm vs 400 nm).
Radio waves from a station are about a billion times longer than the X-rays used in a clinic.

boxes.text: Why do astronomers look at all kinds of light? Different matter interacts with different light. A brick wall blocks visible light but lets radio waves through (that is why radios and phones work indoors), so each type of light carries different information about distant objects.
Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-ray, Gamma, from longest to shortest wavelength.

The word radiation only means energy spreading out; it is not always dangerous. Radio waves and X-rays are both light, they differ only in wavelength, frequency and energy, never in speed. You cannot hear radio waves: a radio device decodes them into sound. Slide 1 of the 5.2 deck is just a title slide with an X-ray image; the explanation of it comes from the textbook.

quiz.q: A radio station at 93.3 FM broadcasts radio waves with a frequency of 93.3 MHz (1 MHz = 10^6 Hz). Using c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, what is the wavelength of these waves?
quiz.why: Radio waves are light, so lambda x f = c and lambda = c / f = (3 x 10^8 m/s) / (93.3 x 10^6 Hz) = 3.2 m. Forgetting the 10^6 in MHz gives 3.2 x 10^6 m; dividing the wrong way round gives 0.31 m.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 5.1 Example 1 (p. 143); Ch5.2 slide 4

quiz.q: The middle of the visible spectrum is green light with a wavelength of 550 nm (1 nm = 10^-9 m). Using c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, what is its frequency?
quiz.why: f = c / lambda = (3 x 10^8 m/s) / (550 x 10^-9 m) = 5.45 x 10^14 Hz, about 550 trillion Hz. Forgetting to convert nanometres gives 5.45 x 10^5 Hz; dividing lambda by c gives the useless 10^-15.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 5.1 Example 2 (p. 143); Ch5.2 slide 4

quiz.q: Why does a glass prism turn a beam of white light into a rainbow?
options: The prism adds new colours to the light as it passes through.
The prism absorbs most of the light and re-emits it in different colours.
The prism scatters the light randomly in all directions.
White light is a mix of many wavelengths, and the prism refracts each wavelength by a different amount.
The prism changes the speed of light into several different speeds in empty space.
quiz.why: White light already contains all the colours. Refraction bends each wavelength differently, so they separate. Nothing is added.
quiz.source: Ch5.1 slide 3; Cosmic Perspective 5.1

quiz.q: Which statement about the interaction of light and matter is INCORRECT?
options: A green lawn looks green because it scatters green light and absorbs most of the other colours.
Dark sunglasses absorb more light and transmit less light than clear eyeglasses.
Air molecules scatter sunlight, which is why shadows on Earth are not completely black.
A red chair looks red because it absorbs red light and scatters all the other colours.
A movie screen scatters light in many directions so that everyone in the room sees the picture.
quiz.why: A red chair scatters red light and absorbs the other colours, so the statement has it backwards. The other four are all correct.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.1 (p. 139, Figure 5.3 and Common Misconceptions p. 140); Ch5.1 slide 4

quiz.q: A laser beam crosses a dusty room and you see its path from the side. The same laser beam in empty space would not be visible from the side. Why?
options: Light only travels in straight lines when there is matter to carry it.
The dust absorbs the laser light and gives off new light of a different colour.
Dust and air molecules scatter some of the laser light toward your eyes; in space there is nothing to scatter it.
Laser light travels faster in air than in space, so it reaches your eyes.
In empty space the laser light is reflected by a mirror-like layer and goes the other way.
quiz.why: You only see light that enters your eye. A beam passing sideways is visible only because some of its light is scattered into your eye by dust or air. In empty space nothing scatters it, so you would not see it unless it was aimed at you.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.1 (p. 140, Common Misconceptions: Light Paths, Lasers and Shadows)

quiz.q: A 100 W light bulb is left on for one full day (86,400 s). About how much energy does it use? (1 W = 1 J/s)
quiz.why: Energy = power x time = 100 J/s x 86,400 s = 8.64 x 10^6 J, about 10 million joules, close to the food energy a person uses in a day. Using 24 hours or 1,440 minutes instead of seconds gives the smaller wrong answers.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.1 (p. 138: 100 W bulb; human need about 10 million J per day); Ch5.1 slide 2

quiz.q: Why does a green object look black when it is lit only by red light?
options: It scatters all the red light into the room.
It reflects only red light, which looks black under red light.
It contains pigments that darken in red light.
It absorbs the red light, so almost no light is sent back to your eye.
It absorbs green light, so it takes in no other light.
quiz.why: An object's colour is the light it sends back. A green object returns green and absorbs the other colours, including red. With only red present, nothing comes back.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q17 (answer B in the explained file); Cosmic Perspective 5.1

quiz.q: Newton sent only the red light from one prism into a second prism. What came out of the second prism?
options: Only red light, which shows the colour belongs to the light and not the prism.
A full rainbow again, which shows the prism makes colour.
Only violet light, because the second prism reverses the colours.
No light at all, because red light cannot be refracted.
White light, because the second prism recombines the colours.
quiz.why: If the prism made the colours, the second prism would also give a rainbow. Red in and only red out shows the colour is a property of the light.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 140, Newton's prism experiment)

quiz.q: Which statement about light is INCORRECT?
options: A light wave is made of vibrating electric and magnetic fields.
Each photon is described by a wavelength, a frequency and an energy.
All photons carry the same energy, because all light travels at the same speed.
A light wave carries energy from place to place without carrying matter along.
Light can make charged particles such as electrons bob up and down.
quiz.why: Every photon does travel at c, but its energy depends on its frequency (E = hf), so a radio photon and an X-ray photon have very different energies. The other statements are all correct.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slides 2, 6, 9; Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (pp. 140-142)

quiz.q: What property of a wave tells you how many peaks pass a given point each second?
quiz.why: Frequency is peaks per second (hertz). Wavelength is the distance between peaks, speed is how fast peaks travel and amplitude is the peak height.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q20; Ch5.2 slide 3

quiz.q: If the wavelength of a light wave doubles, what happens to its frequency and photon energy?
options: The frequency is cut in half and the energy is cut in half.
The frequency doubles and the energy doubles.
Nothing changes, since all light travels at the same speed.
The frequency is cut in half, but the energy doubles.
The frequency and energy both increase by a factor of 4.
quiz.why: Since c = λf is fixed, doubling λ halves f. Since E = hf, halving f halves E.
quiz.source: ASTR207 practice Q24; Ch5.2 slides 4 and 6

quiz.q: Which of these has the highest-energy photons?
quiz.why: Energy rises as wavelength gets shorter. Of the choices X-rays have the shortest wavelength and so the highest photon energy.
quiz.source: ASTR207 practice Q23; Ch5.2 slides 6 and 8

quiz.q: Which statement about radio waves is TRUE?
options: They are a type of sound wave.
They are a form of light and travel at the speed of light.
They travel more slowly than visible light.
They carry more energy per photon than X-rays.
They need air to travel through.
quiz.why: Radio waves are light with a very long wavelength. All light travels at c in empty space, and radio photons have the least energy.
quiz.source: ASTR207 practice Q22; Cosmic Perspective 5.2

quiz.q: The picture shows three light waves. Suppose each wave is a single photon of light. Which photon carries the most energy and which the least?
options: The 1 cm photon has the most energy and the 0.25 cm photon the least.
The 0.25 cm photon has the most energy and the 1 cm photon the least.
The 0.5 cm photon has the most energy and the 0.25 cm photon the least.
All three have the same energy, because all light travels at the same speed.
They cannot be compared without knowing the height of each wave.
quiz.why: The shortest wavelength has the highest frequency (1 cm gives 30 GHz, 0.5 cm gives 60 GHz, 0.25 cm gives 120 GHz), and E = hf grows with frequency. So 0.25 cm is the most energetic and 1 cm the least.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 142, 'Think about it' on Figure 5.6); Ch5.2 slide 4

img.alt: Three waves drawn one above the other: 1 cm wavelength, half a centimetre and a quarter of a centimetre.

quiz.q: A photon has a frequency of 5 x 10^14 Hz. Using h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s, what is its energy?
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slide 6

quiz.q:
Compare red light (700 nm) and violet light (400 nm).
I. Red light has the longer wavelength.
II. Violet light has the higher frequency.
III. Red photons carry more energy than violet photons.
quiz.why: Red has the longer wavelength, so by c = λf violet has the higher frequency, and by E = hf violet photons carry more energy, so III is false.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slides 5 and 6

quiz.q: How many times more energy does a violet photon (400 nm) carry than a red photon (700 nm)?
quiz.why: E = hc/λ, so energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. Ratio = 700/400 = 1.75.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slides 5 and 6

quiz.q: Which list puts these kinds of light in order of INCREASING wavelength?
options: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, radio waves
radio waves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
X-rays, gamma rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, radio waves
visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays, infrared, radio waves
infrared, radio waves, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
quiz.why: Wavelength gets longer from gamma rays (shortest) to radio waves (longest). Option b lists them from longest to shortest.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slide 8; Cosmic Perspective Figure 5.7

quiz.q: Red light at the edge of what we can see has a wavelength of 700 nm. A photon with twice the energy of a 700 nm photon has a wavelength of about
quiz.why: E = hc / lambda, so twice the energy needs half the wavelength: 700 / 2 = 350 nm. That is shorter than violet (400 nm), so it is ultraviolet. Doubling the wavelength would halve the energy instead.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slides 5 and 6; Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 142)

quiz.q: The Sun's power output is 3.8 x 10^26 W. How much energy does the Sun radiate in one minute?
quiz.why: 1 W = 1 J/s, so the Sun gives off 3.8 x 10^26 J every second. In 60 s: 3.8 x 10^26 x 60 = 2.28 x 10^28 J. Using 3,600 s gives 1.4 x 10^30 J, and dividing by 60 gives 6.3 x 10^24 J.
quiz.source: Ch5.1 slide 2; Cosmic Perspective 5.1 (p. 138)

quiz.q: A light wave's wavelength drops to one-third of its old value. What happens to the energy of each photon?
options: It becomes nine times as large
quiz.why: One-third the wavelength means 3 times the frequency (c = λf), and E = hf so the energy also becomes 3 times larger.
quiz.source: Ch5.2 slides 4 and 6; Cosmic Perspective Figure 5.6

quiz.q: Why do radios and cell phones work inside a building even though you cannot see through the walls?
options: Radio waves travel faster than visible light, so they push through bricks.
Radio waves are sound waves, which pass through solid walls easily.
Radio waves carry more energy per photon than visible light.
A brick wall is opaque to visible light but transmits radio waves.
The walls emit radio waves of their own.
quiz.why: Different types of light interact differently with matter. A brick wall is opaque to visible light but transmits radio waves, which is why radios and cell phones work inside buildings.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 143: brick wall opaque to visible light but transmits radio waves)

quiz.q: Which statement about electromagnetic radiation is correct?
options: The word radiation always means that the energy is harmful to the body.
Radio waves are sound waves that are too quiet for us to hear.
An X-ray picture shows the X-rays themselves because we can see them.
Only visible light carries radiative energy; radio waves and X-rays carry none.
A radio is a device that decodes radio waves, which are a form of light, into sound.
quiz.why: Radio waves are long-wavelength light, not sound. A radio receiver turns the encoded signal back into sound. Radiation just means energy that spreads out, and it is harmful only when photons carry enough energy to damage tissue. X-rays are invisible; the picture records the ones that pass through.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 142, Common Misconceptions boxes)

quiz.q:
Which of these statements about photon energy are correct?
I. Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to damage skin cells.
II. Radio photons carry enough energy to cause sunburn.
III. X-ray photons carry enough energy to pass through skin and muscle.
quiz.why: Ultraviolet and X-ray photons have short wavelengths and high energy. Radio photons have very little energy and cannot cause sunburn.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective 5.2 (p. 142)

quiz.q: What is the energy of one visible-light photon with a wavelength of 550 nm? (h = 6.626 x 10^-34 J s, c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, 1 nm = 10^-9 m)
quiz.why: E = hc / lambda = (6.626 x 10^-34 J s)(3 x 10^8 m/s) / (550 x 10^-9 m) = 1.99 x 10^-25 / 5.5 x 10^-7 = 3.6 x 10^-19 J. Forgetting to convert nm to metres gives 3.6 x 10^-28 J; multiplying by lambda instead of dividing gives 1.1 x 10^-31 J.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 5.1 Example 3 (p. 143); Ch5.2 slide 6

quiz.q: Suppose all 100 W of a bulb's power left it as 550 nm photons, each with energy 3.6 x 10^-19 J. About how many photons would it send out each second?
quiz.why: 100 W is 100 J every second. Photons per second = (100 J/s) / (3.6 x 10^-19 J per photon) = 2.8 x 10^20. Dividing 3.6 x 10^-19 by 100 instead gives 3.6 x 10^-21, the fraction of the bulb's energy that one photon carries.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 5.1 Example 3, Step 3 (the photon is barely a billion-trillionth of 100 J); idealised all-550 nm assumption is an extension (outside source)

quiz.q: Mercury is 0.387 times as far from the Sun as Earth is. Compared with Earth, about how much more sunlight energy falls on each square metre of Mercury per second?
quiz.why: Sunlight energy per unit area falls with the square of the distance, so the ratio is 1 / 0.387^2 = 1 / 0.150 = 6.7. Forgetting the square gives 1 / 0.387 = 2.6; cubing gives 17.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 10.1 (p. 282: sunlight per unit area declines with the square of distance); Table 10.2 (Mercury 0.387 AU)

quiz.q: A small lamp lights a wall 2 m away. The wall is moved to 6 m from the lamp. How much light energy per second does each square metre of the wall now receive compared with before?
quiz.why: The distance is 3 times larger and the light thins out with the square of the distance, so each square metre gets 1/3^2 = 1/9 as much. Answering 1/3 forgets the square.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 10.1 (p. 282) and Figure 4.17 (inverse-square idea); lamp-and-wall numbers (outside source)

quiz.q: If an incandescent light bulb shines through a glass prism, what would we see?
options: A rainbow, practically identical to what we would get if we shone sunlight through the prism
A single, yellowish colour matching the wavelength output by the light bulb
A rainbow with more reddish colours present than in sunlight's rainbow
A series of spectral lines, indicating what chemicals are present in the light bulb filament
Nothing, since refraction in a glass prism works only with sunlight
quiz.why: A hot filament gives off light of all visible wavelengths, so the prism spreads it into a continuous rainbow (not lines, not one colour, and a prism works on any white light). The filament is only about 3000 K, cooler than the Sun (5800 K), so its light is weighted toward the red end.
quiz.source: Practice test 2 Q22 (answer D in the explained file); Ch5.1 slide 3; the redder balance uses Wien's law (Cosmic Perspective Math Insight 5.2)

quiz.q:
Study the figure of the electromagnetic spectrum. Going from gamma rays toward radio waves, which of these increase?
I. The wavelength
II. The frequency
III. The energy of each photon
quiz.why: The arrows in the picture show wavelength getting longer (shorter to longer) while frequency and energy get lower. So only the wavelength increases. By c = lambda f and E = hf, frequency and energy move together and opposite to wavelength.
quiz.source: Cosmic Perspective Figure 5.7 (p. 143); Ch5.2 slide 8

img.alt: The electromagnetic spectrum from gamma rays on the left to radio waves on the right, with scales for wavelength, frequency and energy.

order.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
order.prompt: Put these kinds of light in order of wavelength, from the shortest at the bottom to the longest at the top.
order.why: Wavelength grows from gamma rays (about the size of an atom or smaller) to radio waves (up to the size of a football field). Frequency and photon energy run the other way: gamma rays have the most, radio waves the least.

order.title: Colours of visible light
order.prompt: Order these colours by wavelength, from the shortest at the bottom to the longest at the top.
order.why: Visible light runs from about 400 nm (violet) to about 700 nm (dark red). Violet and blue have the shortest wavelengths and the most energy per photon; red has the longest wavelength and the least energy.

order.title: Size of the wavelength
order.prompt: Light waves come in many sizes. Order these things, whose sizes match the wavelengths of different kinds of light, from the smallest to the largest.
order.why: In the spectrum picture a hydrogen atom matches the wavelength of X-rays, a protein the ultraviolet, a bacterium visible light, a pinhead the infrared, a baseball microwaves and a football field radio waves.

order.title: Energy of one photon
order.prompt: You want the energy of one photon of 550 nm light. Put the steps in order, first at the bottom and last at the top.
order.why: Units come first: nanometres must become metres. Then f = c / lambda gives the frequency, E = h x f turns it into energy, and the result is stated in joules (3.6 x 10^-19 J).

sort.title: What does matter do to the light?
sort.prompt: Sort each example by the main thing that happens to the light.

items.text: Light passing through a window pane
Light passing through the air of a room
Red glass letting red light through
Your hand warming near a light bulb
Cells in your eye detecting light
A green object looking black under red light
A mirror sending light along one simple path
A movie screen sending light to every seat
A red chair giving back red light

sort.why: Transmission lets light pass through, absorption takes its energy in (often as heat), and reflection or scattering sends it back out. Snow does both: it absorbs some light, which helps it melt, but scatters most, so it looks bright.

sort.title: More or less energy than visible light?
sort.prompt: Sort each kind of light by whether its photons carry more or less energy than visible-light photons.

items.text: The light used to image bones
The signal from a radio transmitter

sort.why: Energy per photon rises as wavelength gets shorter. Everything shorter than visible (ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays) has more energy; everything longer (infrared, microwaves, radio) has less.

sort.title: Same for all light, or different?
sort.prompt: Sort each property by whether it is the same for every kind of light or different from one kind to another.

items.text: Being made of electric and magnetic fields
Behaving as a stream of photons
Whether our eyes can see it

sort.why: All light travels at c, so wavelength times frequency is always c. Radio waves and X-rays are both light and are both photon streams; they differ only in wavelength, frequency and energy, and so in how they interact with matter.
